entries.html:
Build to Throw Away

As easy as it is to build, it's just as easy to throw away.

Spent a good chunk of this morning remapping Stock Up Dinners against the new understanding of what the product actually needs to be — and landed on the conclusion that the existing build has to be gutted. Not patched. Not extended. Rebuilt from a new foundation.

This isn't a failure. It's the natural consequence of building before designing. The work moved fast; the direction was wrong. When the foundation is wrong, there's no reasonable expectation the thing on top of it will succeed. Better to recognize it early and reset than to keep building on a cracked slab.

The lesson: be ready to throw it away. Not recklessly — but without attachment. The hard work is appropriate design and putting the elements in the right places. Speed of execution only matters if the execution is pointed at something real.

AI Architecture Is the Missing Piece

Had a conversation with Rabbi Leban today through Colorado AI Lab. What stood out: people can intuit that AI has clear benefits for their organization — they feel it. What they're missing is the architecture.

The questions that come up are real and disorienting: Do I throw everything away? Do I rebuild? Do I add new tools on top of what I have? Do I just improve what's already there?

Organizations need a way to think about this, not just a list of tools. The worst thing you can do is throw a bunch of AI solutions at someone who doesn't yet understand the problem they're solving for. The tools are the easy part. The architecture — understanding which problems to solve, in what order, with what approach — is where the actual value is created.

That's the work Colorado AI Lab is positioned to do.

Working on 016 today and hit a clarifying moment that's worth recording.

AI Speeds You Up Into the Wrong Place

AI is a powerful accelerator — but it accelerates you toward building, not toward thinking. The risk is that you move fast into the wrong direction before you've done the hard work of understanding the process your users actually go through.

That's what happened here. The early hours went into designing an app — menus, meal types, one-off cooking vs. weekly prep. It felt like progress. It looked like progress. But it was building the end product before understanding the entry point.

The Real Unlock: Pantry Tracking

The core insight today: the most valuable thing Stock Up Dinners can do is not tell people what to cook — it's tracking what they already have.

Once the pantry is tracked: - Shopping lists write themselves (buy what you're actually missing) - Recipe recommendations become immediately relevant (use what's already there) - The product gets smarter the more someone uses it

Everything else — the 14 meal plans, the Costco shopping list lead magnet, the recipe browsing — these are acquisition surfaces. The pantry tracker is the retention engine and the value core.

Process Before Product

The lead magnet work (Costco staples list + 14 meals) turned out to be generative, not just promotional. Building it forced the question: after someone downloads this and cooks a few meals, what does the ongoing relationship with this product look like?

That question led directly to pantry tracking as the answer.

The lesson isn't to skip product thinking — it's to start with the user's ongoing process, not the final feature set. The app design got complicated because it started in the wrong place. Now there's a clear foundation to rebuild from.

Milestone: 20 reps. And with it, the first real sense of rep fatigue — not from volume, but from a pattern emerging in how reps stall.

The Holding-Pattern Problem

Reps seem to hit a plateau state where progress requires one of two things:

  1. Product execution — building new features, improving the core experience. 002 is the example here: it's live, but the next level requires shipping more functionality. That work falls on the human.

  2. Active selling — going out and closing. 014 is the example: the funnel exists, the assets are ready, but someone has to actually send the messages and get on calls. That also falls on the human.

Both bottlenecks currently require human execution, and at 20 reps, those accumulate faster than they clear.

018 is the outlier — it's in a stable holding state that doesn't demand either. It just exists and works. That's a different kind of rep.

The Question

Is there a useful new categorization for reps in this plateau state? Something beyond live that signals what kind of human action is blocking the next level — execution vs. selling? And is there an AI leverage point that could absorb one or both of those gaps over time?

No answers yet. Just noticing the shape of the problem at 20 reps.

First field note. The pattern across 011 and 014 is the same: I keep building the product and not the distribution. Cold outreach by hand is the only thing that's ever moved a needle.

This realization is the seed of distribution-beats-craft.
